title: Greeting the Class
prompt: You enter the classroom at 9 a.m. Which greeting is appropriate for this time of day?
explanation: At 9 a.m., it is morning, so “Good morning, everybody!” is appropriate. “Good afternoon” and “Good evening” refer to later times of day; “Good night” is usually used when saying goodbye or going to bed.

title: Introducing Yourself
prompt: You are meeting a class for the first time. You want to tell the students that you are their new English teacher. Which statement expresses this?
options: I was your English teacher last year.
I'm a student in this English class.
I'm going to teach you mathematics.
explanation: “I'm your new English teacher” clearly introduces the speaker as the class's new English teacher. The other options describe a former teacher, a student, or a teacher of a different subject.

title: Checking Attendance
prompt: You are taking attendance at the beginning of the lesson. What should you ask?
explanation: “Who is absent today?” asks which students are missing from the current lesson. The other questions refer to a different day or ask about lateness rather than absence.

title: Asking for Silence
prompt: The lesson is about to begin, but some students are still talking. What should you say?
options: Let's continue the lesson with the dialogue.
It's time to finish today's lesson.
It's time to begin, please stop talking.
You may discuss the lesson with your partner.
explanation: “It's time to begin, please stop talking” both announces the start of the lesson and asks students to stop talking. The other options discuss continuing, ending, or allowing conversation.

title: Settling the Class
prompt: The students are noisy and restless before the lesson. What should you say to calm them down?
options: Settle down now so we can start.
explanation: “Settle down now so we can start” asks the class to become calm and ready before the lesson begins. The other responses give instructions for lesson activities without directly addressing the noise and restlessness.

title: Dealing with a Late Student
prompt: A student arrives ten minutes late. You want to ask about the delay. What should you say?
options: We will start in ten minutes.
We started ten minutes ago. What have you been doing?
We have ten minutes left. What have you finished?
explanation: “We started ten minutes ago. What have you been doing?” makes it clear that the lesson has already begun and asks the late student to account for the delay. The other options describe a future start, an early arrival, or completed work.

title: Showing Concern
prompt: David missed school yesterday because he was ill. Today he has returned to class. You want to ask specifically whether his health has improved. What should you say?
options: How are you getting on with your homework?
Are you ready for today's lesson, David?
Have you finished your homework, David?
Are you feeling better today, David?
explanation: “Are you feeling better today, David?” directly asks whether David's health has improved since he was ill. The other options ask about homework or readiness for the lesson, not his recovery.
